name: Istanbul Judeo-Spanish
catalog_citation: Hualde, José Ignacio & Mahir Şaul. 2011. Istanbul Judeo-Spanish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(1): 89–110 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100310000277
catalog_quote: Stress is lexically contrastive in Istanbul Judeo-Spanish, e.g. pera /ˈpera/ ‘pear’, perro /ˈper̆o/ ‘dog’ vs. Perá /peˈra/ (name of a neighborhood), parás /paˈras/ ‘money’, pashá /paˈʃa/ ‘dear child’. Like in all Spanish varieties, stress may fall on any of the last three syllables of the word. There are, however, relatively few nominal forms with antepenultimate stress: lágrima /ˈlagrima/ ‘tear’, múzika /ˈmuzika/ ‘music’. Many nouns with antepenultimate stress in Mainstream Spanish, instead, in Istanbul Judeo-Spanish have final stress: pasharó /paʃaˈro/ ‘bird’, numeró /numeˈro/ ‘number’, guerfanó ‘orphan’, albondigás ‘meat balls’, cf. MSp pájaro, número, huérfano, albóndigas, cf. also arvolé ‘tree’(MSp árbol). ... The shift of the stress from antepenultimate to final position may have taken place under the influence of Turkish and, for cognate words, such as numeró, French. Antepenulti…
sweep_summary: ladi1251 (Ladino/Istanbul Judeo-Spanish, catalog_kind 'lexical' from Hualde & Şaul 2011 JIPA p. 104). The sweep produced a single title hit: Domínguez Caparrós 2009 'The metrics of Sephardic song' (John Benjamins, doi:10.1075/lfab.2.18dom). Its Crossref abstract shows it is about the versification of Sephardic songs (syllable counts, heterometry, stanza forms, rhyme) — prosody-but-not-word-stress; full text is closed (benjamins.com 403, OpenAlex is_oa=false), abstract only; silent on the catalog coding; acquisition priority none. Supplementary API checks (Crossref bibliographic search 'Judeo-Spanish stress accent'; OpenAlex on the wishlisted Bradley 2021 chapter, closed) surfaced no open, first-hand statement of Judeo-Spanish word stress beyond the held Hualde & Şaul 2011, whose p. 104 'Stress' passage was re-located verbatim in the held text file. Catalog coding unchanged; best_new_statement found=false. Metadata with.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are both verbatim on p. 104, section 'Stress', of the held Hualde & Şaul 2011 JIPA PDF, matching the stated locator (Figure 10, fn. 20). sources.citation: Domínguez Caparrós, José. 2009. The metrics of Sephardic song. In Jean-Louis Aroui & Andy Arleo (eds.), Towards a Typology of Poetic Forms: From language to metrics and beyond (Language Faculty and Beyond 2), 355–370. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/lfab.2.18dom
sources.tag: not read: abstract or record only
sources.access_detail: only an abstract or snippet reachable
sources.quote: After briefly presenting the literary genre of Sephardic song (18th–20th centuries), we comment on its principal metrical characteristics, which concern syllabism, the stanza, and rhyme. [...] Some striking features of the meter of Sephardic songs are: the important presence of heterometry, the vitality of the dodecasyllable (a reinterpretation of the accentual verse of Juan de Mena ...) and the vigour of the octosílabo (the French heptasyllable).
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement. The abstract (the only part reachable: benjamins.com returned HTTP 403, OpenAlex reports no open copy) describes verse metrics of Sephardic songs — syllable counts (dodecasyllable, octosyllable), heterometry, stanza forms (zéjel, Purim stanza) and rhyme — situated in the history of Spanish versification. Literary metrics, not phonology; the Glottolog noise_flag is correct.
